description: For All Mankind is a team of students decidated to understanding and exploring the surface of the Moon through open data and crafted tools. From understanding how lunar probes safely land on its surface to designing efficient wheels, tracking celestial bodies from the moon and debating the future of human space exploration, we will investigate astronomical and technological concepts that were previously beyond human reach.
summary:
Where’s My Sun? is an interactive, web-based lunar simulation platform that explores the challenges of predicting solar illumination and Earth visibility across the Moon’s surface. Combining an accessible, visually engaging interface with astronomical modelling and NASA datasets, the platform transforms complex orbital and positional data into an intuitive exploration experience.

Users can navigate a 3D lunar environment, with displayed geographical coordinates, and track the Sun’s azimuth and elevation, calculate solar irradiance and illumination percentages, and monitor sunrise, sunset and Earth visibility. By integrating NASA’s Horizons API, lunar topographical data and historical Apollo and other mission archives, the simulation connects scientific calculations with real lunar exploration, as a potential application for the future.

Designed for both accessibility and technical exploration, "Where’s My Sun?" bridges astronomical science and interactive engineering visualisation, offering an engaging platform for understanding the logistical challenges of sustainable lunar exploration. It allows application for recharging solar powered rovers or landers, lunar plant bases with photosynthesising needs and even surface-to-earth communication by tracking both the Earth and the Sun's accurate positions as seen from the distant rocky surface.
details:
Where’s my sun?

Where’s my sun? is an interactive, web-based simulation platform designed to help users understand how to track the Sun using the Luner terrain and Earth in reference. Unlike any conventional lunar visualisations that simply display the Moon's surface, our platform combines astronomical data and calculations to allow users to explore location on the Moon, monitor changing sunlight conditions, and understand how the availability of essential resources affects mission operations.

What it does:

The simulator provides an interactive representation of the lunar surface, displaying the Sun and Earth relative to the user's selected lunar location. It uses astronomical calculations and lunar mapping data to:

  • Track the Sun's position and movement across the horizontal horizon.
  • Calculate the percentage of sunlight and solar irradiance.
  • Show the time until sunrise/sunset
  • Display lunar lat/long coordinates, surface elevation and illumination conditions.
  • Locate Earth azimuth and degree, with 6 hour calculations.

Benefits and Intended Impact:

  • Accessible design promotes scientific understanding - Helps beginners and students understand the connection between lunar astronomy, solar illumination and the Moon's day-night cycle while program's accuracy through API and calculations can be applied by experts.
  • Illustrates the importance of sunlight for lunar rovers to tell time and recharge and how the location of the Sun in relation to Earth and the Moon for eclipses.
  • Simplifies complexity of lunar surface: Converts astronomical data and engineering calculations into game-like scenario where user can explore the surface with accurate sun/earth positions, size and elevation.
  • Supports future lunar exploration: Introduces the challenges that space agencies must consider when planning long-duration lunar missions and sustainable habitats through comparison and exploration of past rover landing sites with historical information.

Technological Tools:

  • NASA Horizons API: Astronomical position data for calculating the live positions of celestial bodies.
  • Python (Pandas, json): Optional data processing and scientific calculations & development of the interactive user interface and simulation.
  • NASA Scientific Visualisation Studio: Moon 3D Models for Web, AR, and Animation
  • NASA Archives for Apollo 15 and Apollo 17 images, sounds, landing timings and lat/long cordinates information.

Unique Elements and Factors:

  • Interactive lunar environment: Combines a visual lunar landscape with the positions of the Sun and Earth, allowing users to explore different lunar locations with no restricted areas.
  • Real-time calculations: Allows users to observe how changing position on the Moon can influence solar light and earth view availability for recharging and communication.
  • Application to real world: Environment can be used to prepare for timing and locating lunar plant bases to maximise sunlight, or radio stations for long distance surface-to-earth communication or recharging lunar rovers with solar panels.
  • Historical exploration: Can incorporate images and archived audio from previous lunar rover missions, connecting historical exploration with future lunar habitation.
